Lansing at a glance

What is different about selling a house in Lansing?

As Michigan's capital, Lansing straddles three counties. Most parcels are in Ingham, some are in Eaton to the west, and some in Clinton to the north, which decides where your deed is recorded. Look at your tax bill first.

The July 2025 estimate is 113,884 residents, 1.1 percent more than the 2020 base. Homes here are valued well under Kentwood's or Livonia's, and only a little over half are owner-occupied, so a good share of sellers are landlords.

Lansing is also the center of a metro area of roughly 473,000 people, the third largest in Michigan. Michigan State University sits in neighboring East Lansing rather than in the city, and the Census counts 39.14 square miles of land inside Lansing itself. Some of that land, such as the airport tract, came under city control through temporary Michigan land-sharing agreements known as 425 agreements, which are not annexations under state law.

How did Lansing get its shape, and which neighborhoods matter to a seller?

Lansing was chosen as the capital in 1847 because it was more central and safer than Detroit, and it was incorporated as a city in 1859. Ransom Olds built Oldsmobile and later REO Motor Car here, and REO Town along Washington Avenue grew up around his factories.

The city is usually described in four sections, and buyers use the same names:

  • Eastside, east of the Grand River, centered on Michigan Avenue and the Frandor shopping center
  • Westside, around the river's curve, the most mixed by income and home type
  • Northwestside, the smallest section, near the Capital Region International Airport
  • Southside, the fourth section

Old Town, with buildings from the mid-1800s, and REO Town, along Washington Avenue, are the two historic districts people mention first. A listing that names its section and nearest corridor is easier for buyers to place.

Who buys houses in Lansing, and what keeps demand steady?

Government, education, insurance and health care keep Lansing's job base broad. A 2018 ranking by the Lansing Economic Area Partnership put the State of Michigan first with about 14,400 jobs, followed by Michigan State University, University of Michigan Health-Sparrow, General Motors, Lansing Community College, McLaren Greater Lansing and Auto-Owners Insurance. Jackson National Life and Delta Dental also appear on that list.

State and university payrolls mean steady renters and first-time buyers, and investors also look for small, older houses. If your house is a rental, expect investor interest first. If it is owner-occupied and updated, the broader market may pay more.

The school picture is mixed. Lansing School District covers most of the city, yet pieces fall into Holt, East Lansing, Okemos, Mason, Waverly, Grand Ledge and DeWitt, so confirm the district by address.

How easy is it to get around Lansing, and does that help a listing?

Lansing is crossed by I-96, I-69, I-496, US-127, M-43 along Saginaw Street and Grand River Avenue, and M-99 on Martin Luther King Jr. Boulevard. Drivers reach Detroit or Grand Rapids in one highway run, which matters to buyers who commute or work for the state.

The Capital Area Transportation Authority runs 33 bus routes, and the Capital Region International Airport has scheduled flights and a UPS freight hub. A house within walking distance of a bus line or the river trail is worth naming in the listing text.

What does the Census say about Lansing housing and income?

The 2020 to 2024 Census figures show a lower-cost market than Kentwood or Livonia. They are the numbers an appraiser or investor will start from.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $128,700
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 53.8%
  • Median gross rent: $993
  • Households: 51,588, with 2.17 persons per household
  • Median household income: $54,382, and 20.1% of residents in poverty

At that price level, one big repair bill takes a large bite out of a sale. Get two contractor quotes on any big item before you decide between listing and selling as-is.

How does Lansing weather affect an older house?

Winters are cold and summers warm and humid. Snow arrives between early November and early April and averages 51.1 inches a season, and the temperature falls to 0 degrees Fahrenheit or lower on about ten nights a year. The city is largely spared the lake-effect snow that hits Grand Rapids.

For an older Lansing house, those numbers point to the usual trouble spots: aging boilers and furnaces, thin attic insulation, frost-damaged porches and wet basements. Buyers pay attention to these items in any inspection report, so a clear service record helps in either a listing or a cash negotiation.

Do Lansing landlords have to register rentals before selling?

Yes. Lansing requires every rental property to be registered with Code Compliance, with the exception of an owner-occupied single-family dwelling. The fee schedule effective July 1, 2024 lists a $235 new registration fee, a $55 per building fee for a change of owner, and a base inspection fee of $175 per building for one and two family structures.

When a rental is sold, the buyer takes on the registration, the inspection history and any open citations. Late fees and failure-to-register fees are listed on the same schedule, so an unregistered rental costs more to sell than a registered one. Ask Code Compliance for the current forms before you list a rental.

Vacant houses face a separate risk. The schedule includes administrative fees for red-tagged properties, emergency board-up and demolition, all of which can be assessed against the parcel.

What does the Lansing property tax calendar look like?

Lansing publishes a yearly assessment cycle, and its 2026 version shows the dates every owner should know. The same pattern repeats each year.

Lansing 2026 assessment cycle, City of Lansing Assessing Department
DateStep
February 14Last day to pay the prior year's winter taxes
February 20Assessment notices mailed
March 9 to 12March Board of Review hearings on valuation
June 1Deadline for a summer principal residence exemption
July 31Residential Michigan Tax Tribunal filing deadline
November 1Deadline for a winter principal residence exemption
December 31Tax day for the following year

The March hearing dates and the other 2026 entries are now in the past, but they fall in the same weeks every year. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when unpaid bills move to the county, because that date decides who you pay at closing.

What happens at closing and after a sale in Lansing?

Your deed goes to whichever of the three county recorders holds the parcel. The state tax on it is $3.75 per $500 of price, a county tax is added on top, and a handful of family transfers escape both. The title company can tell you which line applies.

Within 45 days of closing the buyer reports the sale to Lansing's assessor, and the house's taxable value is rebased for the following year. You, meanwhile, have 90 days after moving out to cancel your homestead school-tax exemption.

Weighing an investor's cash offer against a listing comes down to the net figure after taxes, recording costs and any city fees.

More questions about Lansing, MI

Which county records a deed for a Lansing house?

The county where the parcel sits records it. Lansing spans Ingham, Eaton and Clinton counties, so read the county on your tax bill and ask that county's register of deeds.

How much is the Lansing rental registration fee?

A new registration costs $235 and a change of owner costs $55 per building under the schedule effective July 1, 2024. Inspections start at a $175 base fee for one and two family buildings.

What is the median home value in Lansing?

Lansing's 2020 to 2024 median home value is $128,700, with median gross rent at $993.

When is the last day to pay Lansing winter taxes?

February 14 is the last day to pay winter taxes, per the city's assessment cycle. Ask the Lansing Treasurer when open bills move to the county.

Do I need to tell the city I sold my house?

The buyer reports the sale to the assessor, and you cancel your homestead exemption within 90 days of moving out.

What makes selling a house in Livonia different from other Michigan cities?

Livonia is a big western suburb, roughly 20 miles northwest of downtown Detroit, where 87.2 percent of housing is owner-occupied. That ratio means most sales are ordinary owner-to-buyer transfers, with a smaller group of rentals that fall under a strict city licensing program.

The Census Bureau estimates 92,603 residents for July 1, 2025, a 3.1 percent drop from the 2020 base of 95,529. In the 2020 count the median age was 45.6, and residents 65 and over made up 21.5 percent.

How did Livonia grow into the city it is now?

Livonia Township was organized in 1835 and named for Livonia, New York, where many early settlers came from. Residents voted to become a city on May 23, 1950, partly to collect tax revenue from the Detroit Race Course, which closed in 1998 and was redeveloped.

Census counts went from 17,634 in 1950 to 66,702 in 1960 and 110,109 in 1970, so a great deal of the housing was built in those postwar years. The city covers about 35.7 square miles of land, with Newburgh Lake and Nankin Lake in the south and southwest linked by Hines Drive.

Gather your permit history before you list. The city issues the permits for additions, decks, basement finishing and similar work, and open permits or violations are tracked by the Inspection Department.

What jobs and schools support the Livonia housing market?

Livonia's largest employers include Ford Motor Company, Trinity Health, Livonia Public Schools, St. Mary Mercy Hospital, Schoolcraft College, ZF Automotive and United Parcel Service. Laurel Park Place, a mall opened in 1989 at Six Mile and Newburgh roads, anchors retail, and former mall sites were redeveloped as Wonderland Village and Livonia Marketplace.

Most addresses fall in Livonia Public Schools, which runs Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. A portion of northeast Livonia is served by the Clarenceville School District. Franklin offers the International Baccalaureate program for select students, Churchill houses a math, science and computer program plus a creative and performing arts program, and Stevenson has a global education school. Madonna University and Schoolcraft College are also in the city.

The district runs two early childhood centers, thirteen elementary schools, four upper elementary schools, three middle schools and three high schools. Frost Middle School hosts the MACAT program for academically talented students, and Webster Elementary hosts a similar program for younger grades.

Confirm which district serves your address before you describe the school zone in a listing.

How do commutes and local amenities shape a Livonia listing?

The mean trip to work is 24.3 minutes, and public bus service is limited, so households here depend on cars. Highway access and garage space are therefore selling points to mention.

The amenities that buyers ask about are easy to document:

  • Four public library locations under the Livonia Public Library
  • The community recreation center on Hubbard Road
  • The Livonia Hockey Association, described as the largest amateur hockey association in Michigan
  • The Livonia Spree, an anniversary fair held each June with food, rides and fireworks

Broadband subscriptions reach 94.5 percent of households, and 41.9 percent of adults hold a bachelor's degree or higher.

What do Census figures show about Livonia housing?

The 2020 to 2024 Census figures put Livonia at the top of the four cities in this group for income and owner share.

Livonia housing and household figures, Census QuickFacts
MeasureLivonia
Median value of owner-occupied homes$281,100
Owner-occupied housing rate87.2%
Median gross rent$1,322
Households38,348
Median household income$98,460
Residents aged 65 and over22.3%
Same house one year ago92.0%

Median monthly owner costs are $1,698 with a mortgage and $678 without one. The 92 percent figure for staying put is the highest of the group, so a house that comes up for sale has often had the same occupants for years.

Does a Livonia rental need a license before it can be sold?

Livonia licenses and inspects rentals, and a rental may not be occupied without a rental license and a Certificate of Compliance. The city's rental guide says licenses renew annually or at title transfer, and inspections happen annually, at a change of tenants or at a change of ownership, whichever comes first.

If you own a rental and plan to sell, the guide spells out these steps:

  • Send the Inspection Department a copy of the purchase agreement so a scheduled renewal can be cancelled.
  • Keep any follow-up inspection already booked so open violations get cleared.
  • Tell the buyers the city will need to inspect if violations remain after title moves.
  • After closing, the new owners take their Property Transfer Affidavit and Homestead Affidavit to the Assessor and then bring copies to the inspectors.

The guide also applies the state occupancy standard of 225 square feet for the first person and 70 for each additional person, not counting baths or closets. Common rental violations in the guide include dryer venting, missing smoke alarms and GFCI outlets, and a furnace carbon monoxide check every three years by a licensed mechanical contractor. Call the Inspection Department at 734-466-2580 for the current fees and wait times, since the guide notes a lead time of about a month.

When are Livonia property taxes due, and who is paid?

Livonia bills real and personal property taxes on July 1 and December 1. The summer bill's deadline is September 14. The Treasurer then splits the collections among the money to the city, two school districts (Livonia and Clarenceville), Schoolcraft College, the state education tax, Wayne County, Wayne RESA and the Oakland ISD.

Delinquent real property taxes go to the Wayne County Treasurer. For outstanding permits, violations, vacant or abandoned registration fees or Certificate of Occupancy questions, the Treasurer's page tells you to call the Inspection Department, because those fees do not show on the online tax inquiry. Special assessment requests go by email to the Treasurer's office.

Check the city's online property inquiry before closing so your title company can see the tax history for the parcel.

How is a Livonia deed recorded and taxed?

Livonia sits inside Wayne County, so the Wayne County Register of Deeds handles recording. A deed first needs the county treasurer's tax certification unless an exemption applies. The register's schedule from January 1, 2026 lists $26 per document plus a $4 survey fee where applicable, and service is by appointment.

Michigan's state transfer tax works out to $3.75 per $500 of sale price, and the Wayne County levy is separate, so the title company should quote both. Gifts to children and grandchildren are among the listed exemptions.

Closing starts two clocks. The buyer has 45 days to report the transfer to Livonia's assessor, and you have 90 days from moving out to cancel a homestead exemption you no longer qualify for.

More questions about Livonia, MI

How many people live in Livonia?

The Census Bureau estimates 92,603 residents for July 1, 2025. That is down 3.1 percent from the April 2020 base.

Who records a deed for a house in Livonia?

The county register of deeds, after the county treasurer certifies the taxes. Service there is by appointment.

When is the summer tax bill due in Livonia?

Billing goes out July 1 for summer, with a September 14 deadline that rolls to the next business day on weekends and holidays. Winter bills follow on December 1.

Does my Livonia rental need an inspection before I sell it?

Send the Inspection Department the purchase agreement so a scheduled inspection can be cancelled or kept to clear violations. The city inspects rentals at a change of ownership, so call 734-466-2580.

Which school districts serve Livonia?

Most of the city is in Livonia Public Schools, which runs Franklin, Churchill and Stevenson high schools. A portion of northeast Livonia is in the Clarenceville School District, so check the district for your address.

Where does a Kentwood home sale begin?

Kentwood sits in Kent County on the southeast side of Grand Rapids, and a sale there follows Michigan's county recording rules plus a few city offices you will deal with directly. Kentwood's July 2025 population estimate is 54,776, which is 0.8 percent above the 2020 base.

Most sellers meet three questions early: what the house might fetch, what the city requires before title moves, and how the tax bill is split at closing. This page answers each with Kentwood's own figures and offices, so any route you choose starts from local facts.

How is Kentwood laid out, and what does that mean for a home sale?

Kentwood covers about 21 square miles of land and is bordered by Wyoming on the west, Grand Rapids and Grand Rapids Township to the north, Cascade Township to the east and Gaines Township to the south. It was incorporated in 1967 out of Paris Township, partly to stop neighboring cities from annexing more land, and it took its name from the Kentwood Public Schools.

Road access shapes how quickly buyers can reach a house. The main routes are:

  • I-96, which clips the northeast corner of the city
  • M-11 along 28th Street, a busy commercial strip
  • M-37 along East Beltline Avenue and Broadmoor Avenue
  • M-6, the southern bypass linking I-196 near Hudsonville with I-96 near the Gerald R. Ford International Airport

Two paths, the Paul Henry Rail Trail and the East-West Trail, run through town, and homes near them tend to be easy to describe in a listing. School boundaries matter too: Kentwood Public Schools serves most addresses, while Forest Hills Public Schools and Kelloggsville Public Schools cover parts of the city. Confirm the district for your street before pricing.

What do the Census numbers say about Kentwood housing?

The Census Bureau's 2020 to 2024 figures describe a city where owners are the majority and median rent runs $1,260 a month. The table lists the figures that bear most on a sale.

Kentwood housing and household figures, Census QuickFacts

About four in ten homes are rented, so many Kentwood sellers are landlords, and the next section covers the rental certificate that affects them. A median value is a midpoint for the whole city. It will not predict your street, so ask for sold comparables from the same school attendance area.

Does winter in Kentwood affect what buyers look for?

Yes, because Kentwood has a warm-summer continental climate with real cold. Mean daily highs in January sit near 30 degrees Fahrenheit and mean lows near 15, and the area gets roughly 34 inches of precipitation across a year, spread fairly evenly from month to month.

Inspectors in town spend their time on the furnace, attic insulation, roof and basement. If one of them is worn out, either repair it before listing or sell as-is at a price that reflects the work. An as-is cash sale hands that repair risk to the buyer. Whatever route you take, get the furnace serviced and keep the receipt, because heating questions come up first in almost every walkthrough.

Does a rental house in Kentwood need a certificate before it changes hands?

A rental dwelling in Kentwood must be registered and hold a valid certificate of compliance, and that certificate stays with the owner who earned it. Under the city's rental dwelling inspection ordinance, a certificate can pass to a buyer only if the sale closes within 90 days of the certificate being issued and the buyer tells the city within 30 days of the sale.

The details that matter to a landlord seller:

  • A six-year certificate does not transfer. If it moves to a new owner inside the 90-day window it reverts to a two-year certificate.
  • Failure by the buyer to notify the city results in suspension of the certificate, and a replacement is dated back to the sale with fees owed from that date.
  • An owner who lives in a condominium unit needs no registration or certification, but a condominium owned as a rental is treated as a single-family rental.
  • Certificates cannot be issued while the property has unpaid city bills.

Call the Inspections Department at 616-554-0700 before you sign a contract on a rental, so the certificate dates and any open violations are known in advance.

When are Kentwood property taxes due, and how do appeals work?

Kentwood mails summer bills in the first week of July, due August 20, and winter bills in the first week of December, due February 14. Unpaid balances move to the Kent County Treasurer on March 1, and a qualifying owner has until September 15 to file a summer deferment with the city.

The assessment side runs on a fixed yearly rhythm:

  • Change notices go out soon after February 1 and carry the appeal dates.
  • The Board of Review begins hearings on the Tuesday after the first Monday in March, by appointment.
  • A homeowner still unsatisfied after the board has until July 31 to petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal.
  • Occupants claim the school-tax exemption on a homestead by June 1 to cover the summer bill, or November 1 for winter.

Appeals cannot rest on a neighbor's lower tax bill. Michigan lets taxable value rise more slowly for long-term owners, so a recent buyer will usually pay more than an owner next door who has held the house for years.

What happens to the tax bill and the exemption after a Kentwood sale?

After the deed records, the buyer owes the Kentwood Assessor a property transfer affidavit within 45 days. Taxable value then resets to the state equalized value for the next tax year, so the buyer's first full bill may look nothing like yours.

As the seller, stop claiming your principal residence exemption by filing the rescission form with the city within 90 days of moving out. Owners who already bought a new Michigan home while the old one sits unsold can ask for a conditional rescission, which Kentwood says may run up to three tax years if the house is never rented. The state form is 4640.

Recording happens downtown in the County Administration Building, 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Two transfer taxes attach to the deed: the state levy of $3.75 per $500 of price, and a county levy that Michigan sets at 55 cents per $500 below 2,000,000 residents. Your title agent should show both on the settlement statement.

Should you list in Kentwood or take an investor's cash offer?

An investor's cash offer usually closes faster and carries fewer conditions, while a listing reaches more buyers but adds showings and lender timelines. Neither is free of cost, so compare net figures.

Before you sign anything, list your own requirements: a closing date, the mortgage payoff and a plan for tenants. Ask each buyer in writing who covers recording costs and whether open city violations stay with the house. The Assessor's online sales search shows qualified Kentwood sales, which helps you judge whether an offer sits near the neighborhood's range.

More questions about Kentwood, MI

How much does the Census say a Kentwood house is worth?

Census data for 2020 to 2024 gives a median owner-occupied value of $268,200 in Kentwood. It is a citywide midpoint only.

Who collects Kentwood property tax, and where do unpaid taxes go?

Kentwood's summer bill is due August 20 and its winter bill February 14. Whatever is still open on March 1 goes to the county.

What paperwork follows a Kentwood sale?

Mostly the buyer's paperwork: the transfer affidavit goes to the assessor. Your part is the rescission of your principal residence exemption, plus a rental certificate check with Inspections if you were a landlord.

Can I sell a Kentwood rental with tenants still living there?

Yes, but the rental certificate must be valid and the buyer must notify the city within 30 days of the sale for a transferred certificate to stay in force. Call Inspections at 616-554-0700 first.

Which county office records the deed for a Kentwood sale?

The Kent County Register of Deeds, downtown at 300 Monroe Avenue NW. Transfer tax is collected at that recording.

What does a seller in Lincoln Park have to do that sellers in most Michigan cities do not?

A Lincoln Park seller needs a Certificate of Approval from the city's Building Department before the house can be transferred. The city's ordinance on inspection of residential dwellings prior to sale makes it unlawful to transfer a dwelling, or to act as a broker for the transfer, without a current certificate.

The rule shapes the timeline of every sale in the city, however you find your buyer. The rest of this page explains how the certificate works, then covers the city, its housing figures and the tax and recording steps that follow.

How does the Lincoln Park Certificate of Approval work?

The ordinance (Chapter 1488 of the city's codified ordinances) requires anyone about to transfer a dwelling to register with the Building Department so an inspection can be scheduled. The fee is set by City Council resolution, so ask the department for the current amount.

The main points of the chapter:

  • A Certificate of Approval is valid for one sale or transfer, and a new inspection is required each time the dwelling is sold again.
  • A dwelling includes the house and accessory uses such as garages, sheds, pools, gazebos and playhouses.
  • A buyer may take responsibility for correcting violations by signing a notarized affidavit filed with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited.
  • Failing to obtain the certificate is a municipal civil infraction with a $500 fine.

Inspectors may enter the premises during normal business hours to inspect, and owners, agents and occupants must give access to every part of the property they control. The enforcing official can also order immediate action to remove a hazard. Clear access to the garage, sheds and any pool or gazebo before the inspection date, because accessory structures are part of what the ordinance covers.

A transfer means a sale, a land contract or the exercise of an option to purchase. Gifts, devises and lien foreclosures are outside the definition. Rentals follow a separate track, covered below.

How are the certificates for owner-occupied and rental houses different?

Lincoln Park uses different certificates for different situations, and sellers sometimes confuse them. The table summarizes the three named in the ordinance.

Certificates in Lincoln Park Chapter 1488, City of Lincoln Park codified ordinances
CertificateApplies toHow long it lasts
Certificate of ApprovalResidential dwelling being sold or transferredOne sale or transfer
Certificate of ComplianceRental dwellings and rental unitsThree years, unless the property is sold first
Certificate of OccupancyApproved use or occupancy under the zoning ordinancesIssued by the Building Department

A rental that holds a current Certificate of Compliance is not treated as a dwelling for the Certificate of Approval rule, but a new inspection and a new Certificate of Compliance are required before a rental is sold or transferred. If you own a rental, schedule that inspection before you sign a contract.

What is Lincoln Park like, and who lives there?

Lincoln Park is a Downriver suburb of Detroit in Wayne County, about 11 miles southwest of downtown. With only 5.84 square miles of land and 6,896 people per square mile in 2020, it ranked second in Michigan for density, behind Hamtramck. By the July 2025 estimate the city has 38,529 residents, down 4.3 percent from the 2020 base.

Its neighbors are Detroit, Allen Park, Melvindale, Ecorse, Wyandotte and Southgate. The north and south branches of the Ecorse River run through town and join before leaving it. Council Point Park marks the 1763 meeting where Pontiac urged tribal leaders to join him against Fort Detroit.

The city was laid out in 1906 as part of Ecorse Township, became a village in 1921 and a city in 1925. It grew as a bedroom community for workers at the River Rouge Plant and other auto and steel works, and two shopping centers opened in 1955 and 1956. Lincoln Park Public Schools serves residents through Lincoln Park High School, Lincoln Park Middle School and seven elementary schools.

What do the Census figures say about Lincoln Park homes?

The 2020 to 2024 figures describe a compact, owner-heavy city with a modest median value.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $131,000
  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 68.8%, with 14,767 households
  • Median gross rent: $1,023
  • Median monthly owner costs: $1,169 with a mortgage, $530 without
  • Same house one year ago: 91.3%
  • Mean commute to work: 24.4 minutes
  • Persons per household: 2.66, the largest of the four cities in this group
  • Residents under 18: 25.5%, also the highest of the four

Those figures, together with a bachelor's degree rate of 11.5 percent and a poverty rate of 21.5 percent, show a price level where a five-figure repair matters a great deal to a net result. Price the house with the inspection list in hand, since a buyer will do the same.

When are Lincoln Park property taxes due?

The city treasurer collects only current-year taxes. Summer bills are mailed by the end of June and fall due August 20, with later installment dates for owners who pay in parts, and a 1 percent penalty applies on the 20th of each month to unpaid summer taxes. Winter bills are mailed around the end of November and are due in mid-February, with a 1 percent monthly penalty after that.

All unpaid taxes transfer to the Wayne County Treasurer on March 1. The processor adds 2.95 percent to online payments, and a duplicate bill costs $10 unless you print the record from the city site. Title companies, agents and landlords are told this in a notice on the city's tax page.

Business personal property is taxed through the same office. Anyone operating on December 31 owes the following year's entire billing cycle, under state law.

How are a Lincoln Park deed and transfer tax handled?

Lincoln Park deeds are recorded by the Wayne County Register of Deeds. The Wayne County Treasurer must certify taxes on a deed first in most cases, and visits are by appointment. The fee schedule that began January 1, 2026 sets a deed at $26, with a $4 survey fee where it applies.

The state tax comes to $3.75 per $500 of price, with a separate county tax. State law exempts some conveyances, for example a deed given in foreclosure and a land contract that has not yet passed title, so ask the title company whether yours qualifies.

Afterward, the buyer sends the assessor a transfer affidavit within 45 days, and your own homestead exemption should be cancelled within 90 days of your move.

More questions about Lincoln Park, MI

Do I need an inspection to sell my house in Lincoln Park?

Yes. Lincoln Park requires a Certificate of Approval from the Building Department before a dwelling is transferred, and a new one for every sale. Register with the department so it can schedule the inspection, and ask what the council-set fee is.

What is the fine for selling without a Certificate of Approval?

The ordinance sets the fine for failing to obtain a Certificate of Approval at $500, as a municipal civil infraction. It also states that other statutory and common-law rights and actions are not limited by that penalty, so a buyer or the city may have further remedies.

Can a buyer take over the violations in Lincoln Park?

Yes, by signing a notarized affidavit that states the buyer's intent to correct them and filing it with the Building Department. If the violations are not corrected within six months, occupancy may be prohibited, so a buyer needs a realistic repair budget and schedule.

What does the Census say a Lincoln Park house is worth?

Lincoln Park's median owner-occupied home value is $131,000 for 2020 to 2024, and median gross rent is $1,023.

When do unpaid Lincoln Park taxes go to the county?

Come March 1, everything unpaid belongs to the county treasurer, and the city no longer takes those payments.
